The Bluespotted seabream (Evynnis ehrenbergii) reaches a maximum length of 43 centimeters [Li = 43 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-bodied sparids common to the eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea. Field surveys of natural populations indicate that adult individuals typically achieve asymptotic body masses approaching 1.2 kilograms [Wwi = 1.2 kilograms], a figure derived from extensive length-weight regression analyses. Interestingly, the onset of gonadal maturation occurs at a relatively modest body size, with females attaining puberty at 19.6 centimeters [Lp = 19.6 centimeters] total length. This length-based threshold is notably lower than that observed in several congeneric species, such as Evynnis tumifrons, where maturation may be delayed until individuals exceed approximately 22 centimeters. The early maturation strategy observed in Evynnis ehrenbergii is likely linked to the relatively high natural mortality rates experienced by younger cohorts, favouring an earlier investment in reproduction. Growth increments slow considerably after the pubertal transition, with most somatic expansion concentrated in the early juvenile phase.

Eggs are released through a broadcast spawning strategy during the warmer months, and at a stable incubation temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the lecithotrophic larvae complete endogenous yolk absorption and undergo eclosion after a period of approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days]. This relatively abbreviated developmental window, compared to sparids spawning in cooler waters, reflects the accelerating effect of elevated thermal conditions on embryonic metabolic rates. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a wet weight at birth of roughly 0.00032 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00032 grams], a minute mass that underscores the extreme vulnerability of the prolarval stage. During this endotrophic phase, the larva relies exclusively on its yolk reserves, and the duration of this non-feeding interval is tightly coupled to water temperature. The small initial body mass also has consequences for the timing of the exotrophic transition, as the window for successful first prey capture is brief under these thermal conditions.

Reproductive output in Evynnis ehrenbergii is substantial for a fish of its size. At a water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], spawning females exhibit a mean fecundity of approximately 274 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 274 eggs per spawning event], a per-event rate derived from batch fecundity estimates performed on gravid individuals collected during the peak of the breeding season. This figure corresponds to roughly 0.77 spawning events per day [F_R_i = roughly 0.77 spawning events per day], indicating that females are capable of nearly continuous vitellogenic cycling during the reproductive window. The high-frequency, low-duration spawning intervals observed in this species are characteristic of warm-water sparids that capitalise on brief pulses of planktonic productivity. Such an iteroparous schedule demands considerable energetic investment, and the energetic costs of gamete production are partially offset by the hyperphagic feeding behaviour displayed by adults in the weeks preceding the spawning season.

Controlled laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a constant temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C] have provided a detailed picture of the species' longevity. Under these conditions, the maximum recorded lifespan reaches 15 years [am = 15 years], a relatively extended duration for a sparid of this body size at a temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C]. For context, several related sparids in the region exhibit maximum longevities of only 8 to 12 years, suggesting that Evynnis ehrenbergii may possess comparatively slower rates of physiological ageing. The oldest individuals in wild populations, identified through otolith annulus readings, have been confirmed at ages approaching 15 years [am = 15 years] as well, indicating that the laboratory-derived estimate accurately reflects natural senescence patterns at a temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C]. Such a lifespan, combined with an early onset of maturity, allows individuals to accumulate multiple reproductive seasons over their lifetime, a life-history configuration that buffers the population against years of poor recruitment.

Comparative physiological studies have highlighted the temperature sensitivity of early life stages in Evynnis ehrenbergii, particularly the tight coupling between thermal regime and developmental milestones. At the standard reference temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the pre-feeding larval duration of 10 days [ab = 10 days] is followed by a rapid growth phase that allows juveniles to recruit to benthic habitats within several weeks. The ultimate total length of 43 centimeters [Li = 43 centimeters] is attained only after several years of steady somatic growth, with the majority of length gain occurring before the onset of reproductive maturity. An adult wet weight of 1.2 kilograms [Wwi = 1.2 kilograms] represents the upper end of the size distribution, with most individuals in exploited populations averaging closer to 0.9 kilograms. The species' growth trajectory and moderate maximum length position it as a typical representative of the demersal sparid community inhabiting rocky and sandy substrates along the Levantine coast.
